title: What exactly happens when two transactions deadlock (A locks row 1 then waits for row 2 while B locks row 2 then waits for row 1), how does InnoDB handle it (it detects the cycle and rolls back one transaction as the victim), and why must the application be ready to RETRY the rolled-back transaction: plus how do you reduce deadlocks (consistent lock ordering, short transactions, proper indexing to lock fewer rows) rather than claiming "deadlocks should never happen"?
shortTitle: Deadlocks: What Happens, How InnoDB Handles Them, and Why You Must Retry

s1_definition.oneliner: A deadlock is a circular lock wait; InnoDB detects the cycle and rolls back one transaction as the victim, so the application must catch the error and retry.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Circular wait** – transaction A holds row 1 and waits for row 2 while transaction B holds row 2 and waits for row 1; neither can proceed.
- **Automatic detection** – InnoDB maintains a wait-for graph, detects the cycle, and immediately rolls back one victim (the cheapest to undo).
- **Application retry** – the victim receives error 1213 (SQLState 40001) and must re-run the whole transaction with bounded retries and randomized backoff.
- **Reduce frequency** – use consistent lock ordering (always lock the lower id first), keep transactions short, and index predicates so fewer rows are locked.
- **Never claim impossible** – deadlocks are a normal, expected outcome under concurrency; robust systems treat them as a retryable condition.
s1_definition.analogy: Two National Bank of India clerks each grab one of two ledgers the other needs: clerk A holds the savings ledger and reaches for the loan ledger, while clerk B holds the loan ledger and reaches for the savings ledger. A supervisor spots this standoff, tells one clerk to drop everything and start over, which frees a ledger so the other finishes. The clerk who was sent back simply tries the whole task again.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Transaction A                    Transaction B
  ─────────────                    ─────────────
  LOCK row 1001 (X) ✓              LOCK row 1002 (X) ✓
       │                                │
       ▼                                ▼
  REQUEST row 1002 ──── WAIT ──── REQUEST row 1001
       │                                │
       └────────── DEADLOCK ────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
              InnoDB detects cycle
              in wait-for graph
                      │
                      ▼
              Victim (B) rolled back
              Error 1213 returned
                      │
                      ▼
              A acquires freed lock
              A completes
              B retries
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A deadlock is a circular wait between transactions: A holds row 1 and requests row 2, while B holds row 2 and requests row 1, forming a cycle in the wait-for graph that neither can escape. InnoDB handles it automatically by maintaining a wait-for graph, detecting the cycle, and immediately rolling back one transaction as the victim, returning error 1213 so the surviving transaction completes.

Because the victim is rolled back, the application must be ready to retry. The correct pattern is to catch the deadlock error (SQLState 40001), re-run the whole transaction a small bounded number of times with randomized backoff, which is safe only because the transaction is written to be fully re-runnable.

To reduce deadlocks, consistent lock ordering is the most effective technique: if every transfer always locks the lower account id first, the circular wait cannot form. Short transactions minimize the window locks are held, and proper indexing ensures only the needed rows are locked.

At the National Bank of India the transfer service deadlocked when opposing transfers locked the same two accounts in opposite order. Rajesh fixed it by making every transfer lock the lower id first and wrapping the transfer in a bounded retry, so any residual deadlock is transparently re-attempted.

Remember one sentence: a deadlock is a circular lock wait that InnoDB resolves by rolling back a victim, so the application must catch the error and retry, and you reduce deadlocks with consistent lock ordering, short transactions, and good indexing.

---

keyPoints: A deadlock is a circular wait where two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.
InnoDB detects the cycle in its wait-for graph and rolls back the cheapest transaction as the victim.
The application must catch error 1213 (SQLState 40001) and retry the rolled-back transaction with bounded attempts.
Consistent lock ordering (always lock the lower id first) prevents the circular wait from forming.
Short transactions minimize the window in which locks are held, reducing overlap probability.
Proper indexing ensures a statement locks only the target rows, not unrelated rows from a scan.
Deadlocks are a normal, expected outcome under concurrency and must never be assumed impossible.
